title: service-grid-orchestrator-interaction-patterns
content:
Purpose
---
Working notes to clarify a lightweight, pragmatic mapping of service responsibilities across the control-plane surface: API gateway, orchestrator, and runtime adapters. Goal: reduce ambiguity about who owns what logic (routing, fallbacks, auth, telemetry), minimize duplicate decision points, and outline how ownership shifts in multi-region failover.

Context / Why this doc
---
We've accumulated several overlapping responsibilities in the control plane: gateway-request routing, orchestrator policy enforcement, and adapter-level fallbacks. This has led to unclear SLIs, duplicated retry logic, and frequent back-and-forth between teams during incidents. The aim here is to propose interaction patterns and a minimal ownership map that is practical to implement in the next quarter.

High-level principles (guiding constraints)
---
- Single source of truth for routing decisions: orchestration layer owns global routing policy state (region preferences, cost tiers, model-version pinning).
- Gateway as the enforcement/translation layer: API Gateway translates external requests to internal RPCs and applies per-request guardrails (auth, quotas, basic validation) but defers policy decisions to orchestrator.
- Adapters are execution-only: runtime adapters manage model-specific runtime concerns (quantization variant, caching, local retries) but do not make top-level routing choices.
- Conservative failure surfaces: prefer deterministic fallbacks in orchestrator; adapters may do fast local retries for transient infra glitches but must escalate to orchestrator for policy-driven fallbacks.
- Observability-first contracts: every cross-boundary call must carry correlation metadata (trace-id, routing-hint, client-tier) and produce structured events the Console can consume.

Surface inventory (quick map)
---
- API Gateway (edge-gateway): external ingress, auth, traffic filtering, per-tenant quotas, streaming translation. Owner: Eng-gateway (SLA: 99.95 edge uptime)
- Orchestrator (control-plane-core): routing policy store, rollout/traffic-split engine, multi-region failover logic, model-version pinning, canary scheduling, admission decisions. Owner: Platform Orchestration team (SLA: 99.9 control-plane API)
- Runtime Adapter Layer (adapters/*): region-local connectors to serving runtimes (hosted, dedicated, private). Responsibilities: instantiate model processes, manage KV cache lifecycle, apply adapter-local batching, run small exponential backoffs on transient errors. Owners: serving-runtime teams per adapter (hosted-adapter, dedicated-adapter, private-adapter).
- Router-side Cache (prefix / KV cache service): global and regional caches used to short-circuit repeated prefixes; shared responsibility: orchestrator owns cache coherence policy, adapters own local cache eviction heuristics.

Interaction patterns (happy path)
---
1) Client -> API Gateway: request arrives with metadata (tenant-id, route config, desired model).
2) Gateway -> Orchestrator: lightweight policy check (is customer allowed, quota check is cached at gateway but authoritative is orchestrator). Gateway attaches routing-hint if present.
3) Orchestrator -> Gateway (sync): returns chosen runtime endpoint(s) and routing decisions (region, cost-tier, fallback plan).
4) Gateway -> Adapter (regional): forwards request with routing decision and trace headers.
5) Adapter executes locally and returns streaming tokens / response. Adapter emits structured events (latency, token-count, error-codes) to telemetry.

Edge cases and failure domains
---
- Orchestrator partial outage: gateway must be able to operate in a degraded mode using last-known-policy (TTL 30s for critical routes, 5m for lower priority). TTL policy must be explicit and revocable.
- Adapter-level persistent failure (region-wide): adapter triggers orchestrator callback (async) indicating a regional degradation; orchestrator initiates policy-level reroute (region fallback) and triggers alert.
- Split-brain policy drift: implement simple optimistic lock with versioned policies. Gateway must include policy-version header; orchestrator rejects policy changes with conflicting base-version.
- Quota divergence: gateway caches quota tokens for low-latency enforcement; orchestrator is authoritative and will reconcile. If discrepancy > threshold (5% usage variance) -> orchestrator issues quota-resync and mark tenant for audit.

Routing policies: who decides what
---
- Region preference (latency first): Orchestrator stores latency and cost profiles and picks region. Gateway must not override.
- Cost-tier gating (e.g., cheaper quantized variant): Orchestrator marks allowed model variants per tenant; Gateway passes tenant hints (tier) but orchestration enforces.
- Fallback sequence: Orchestrator defines ordered fallback chain (same-region variants -> other-region same-tier -> lower-tier cheap variant -> cached-response). Adapter may attempt N local retries (N=2) before returning transient error.

Adapter responsibilities (detailed)
---
- Local batching window logic (configurable by adapter): default 8ms for interactive routes, 50ms for throughput jobs.
- Token-level accounting and attribution (per-request).
- Local retry/backoff for infra transient errors (exponential, cap 300ms); after that escalate to orchestrator.
- Implement a minimal healthcheck endpoint that reports readiness + model-cache hit rate + quantized-compat flags.
- Respect orchestrator-supplied policy headers: model-version, trace-id, routing-hint, disable-kv-cache=true.

Ownership map (one-liners)
---
- Routing policy store: orchestrator
- Policy evaluation (global): orchestrator
- Per-request guardrails (auth/quota pre-check): gateway (enforce), orchestrator (audit/authority)
- Model rollout scheduling: orchestrator
- Adapter runtime tuning and kernel selection: serving-runtime teams
- Multi-region failover orchestration: orchestrator
- Emergency switch/fallback script (runbook): platform-sre ops (with orchestrator API)

Telemetry & SLO alignment
---
Minimum signals (for every request): trace-id, policy-version, region, adapter-id, model-version, start_ts, end_ts, token_count, error_code.
SLIs: request_p99_latency_by_route, adapter_success_rate, orchestrator_policy_lookup_latency (p95 < 20ms), gateway_auth_latency (p95 < 8ms).

Decision log (quick)
---
- 2025-12-03: Agreed orchestrator is the single source of truth for routing (Ravi).
- 2025-12-07: Gateway to cache policies for 30s TTL for edge availability (Leah).
- 2026-01-11: Adapter local retries capped at 2 attempts before escalation (Emma).

Open questions / action items
---
- How do we version and migrate policies with long-lived routes (tenant pins)? Proposal: policy-versions + rollout window + forced-expire API. ACTION: Leah to prototype policy version header flow (INF-3421).
- Should adapters be allowed to choose alternate model-variants purely for latency reasons without orchestrator approval? My leaning: no — must request explicit fallback chain. ACTION: Ravi to draft adapter API change.
- Define exact TTLs for cached policies per route class (interactive vs batch). ACTION: team to propose defaults in next weekly sync.

Appendix: quick ASCII mapping (for whiteboard)
---
[Client] -> [API Gateway] -> (policy-check) -> [Orchestrator <-> Policy Store] -> (routing decision) -> [Regional Adapter pool] -> [Serving Runtime]

Notes to self
---
Keep this doc small and prescriptive. If we end up adding every exception here it becomes another spec that nobody reads. Circulate to gateway/orchestrator leads and iterate.

References
---
- Existing artifacts: control-plane-surface-inventory (Confluence), orchestration-api design PR (github above), INF-3421 (policy-version flow).
